# Data findings (auto-generated by `python -m oytra.analysis`)

Cleaned dataset: 1987 labelled COD orders, 01 Apr 2026 – 30 Sep 2026. Overall RTO 28.4% (565 orders). Average order value in data ₹920 (brief says ₹649).

Cleaning: 30 exact duplicate rows removed; status labels normalised (e.g. 'Rto', 'delivered'); 1 IN_TRANSIT order dropped; 12 missing pincodes, 4 missing cities, 17 phones that are not 10-digit mobiles, 3 ₹0 orders, 4 rows where prior RTOs > prior orders (kept, flagged).

## 2. Bad addresses are the strongest single red flag — Hinglish is NOT
| addr_kind     |   orders | rto_rate   |
|:--------------|---------:|:-----------|
| unusable      |      183 | 61.7%      |
| landmark_only |      391 | 30.4%      |
| complete      |     1413 | 23.6%      |

'unusable' = '.', 'xyz', 'call me', 'near station', 'home' or just a city name. Hinglish landmark addresses (e.g. 'Hanuman Mandir ke saamne'): 31.0% RTO on 481 orders vs 27.6% for the rest — so the LLM must judge *completeness*, not penalise language.


## 3. Fake names exist and mostly refuse
44 orders with names like 'Test Order', 'qwerty', 'asdf', 'aaa': 63.6% RTO vs 27.6% for real names. Top: Test Order (11), qwerty (7), na (5), asdf (5), abc (4).

## 6. The money: a delivered order is worth ~2-4x an RTO loss
RTO loss = ₹65+₹65+₹25+8%×₹180 = ₹169.4. A delivered ₹649 order earns 62% margin minus ₹90 shipping+packing = ₹312.4. The ₹300 CAC is acquisition spend already made, not value created by delivering, so it is NOT added. Cancelling only pays when RTO risk exceeds V/(V+L) = 65% (same for first-time and repeat buyers). At the brief's 28% COD RTO, each COD order loses on average ₹47.4 to RTO.

|:-----------------------|--------------------:|:-----------|--------------:|:---------------------|:-----------------------------|
| Claw Clip Set          |                 503 | 29.6%      |           133 | 30.1%                | 74%                          |
| Microfiber Hair Towel  |                 463 | 28.9%      |           116 | 37.1%                | 75%                          |
| Heatless Curling Set   |                 453 | 31.3%      |           129 | 36.4%                | 72%                          |
| Satin Pillowcase       |                 452 | 25.9%      |           131 | 29.0%                | 71%                          |
| Satin Bonnet           |                 451 | 25.3%      |           118 | 23.7%                | 74%                          |
| Scrunchies 6pk         |                 436 | 25.9%      |           111 | 26.1%                | 75%                          |
| Hair Oil 100ml         |                 431 | 29.7%      |            97 | 37.1%                | 77%                          |
| Rice Water Shampoo Bar |                 388 | 27.6%      |            94 | 26.6%                | 76%                          |

Basket size is not monotonic: 1 item 30.8%, 2–3 items 25.2%, 4 items 36.4% (only 107 orders). The model keeps the simple `single_item` flag. Product differences mostly overlap with basket size and value (over 70% of each product's orders are multi-item); adding 8 product flags to the model did not reliably help (section 9). **Rule: we never cancel or hold an order because of which product it contains.** Product mix may later steer *which* prepaid offer to show, never whether to ship.


## 8. Customer-history fields: inconsistent with the file, kept with care
`customer_prior_orders` / `customer_prior_rto` come with each order (like Shopify customer fields). Checked against the same phone's earlier orders in this file (only outcomes ≥14 days old counted as known):

- 364 phones place more than one order (871 orders).
- 238 orders report fewer prior orders than the file itself shows; 203 say 'first-time' although an earlier order exists; on 204 phones the count goes *down* over time.
- 139 orders follow a known RTO on the same phone; only 27 report prior RTO > 0.
- 4 rows have prior RTO > prior orders; 4 of them are RTO.
- Where the file shows no earlier order, RTO by reported prior RTO: 0 → 405/1420, 1 → 16/47, 2 → 13/14.
- Real in-file history points the same way, more weakly: after a known RTO the next order is 29.5% RTO vs 24.5% after a delivery.

Reading: the file is a ~2,000-order sample covering six months of a store with ~1,650 COD orders a month, so missing history is expected; counts that fall over time are not, so the fields are noisy, Root cause in section 10: the counts follow order_id order, not time order (a source-data issue, not our parsing). The 13/14 cell is a small-n warning sign of possible leakage, not proof. Decision and model comparison in section 9.


## 9. Model with / without history and products (`python -m oytra.variants`)
|                                     |   Sep test AUC |   Apr–Aug CV AUC |   Brier |   Sep est. net ₹ (base) |
|:------------------------------------|---------------:|-----------------:|--------:|------------------------:|
| production (reported history)       |          0.738 |            0.699 |  0.1643 |                    1387 |
| no customer history                 |          0.689 |            0.662 |  0.1716 |                    1452 |
| history rebuilt from this file only |          0.694 |            0.659 |  0.1715 |                    1251 |
| reported + rebuilt history          |          0.738 |            0.697 |  0.1645 |                    1510 |
| + 8 product flags                   |          0.747 |            0.69  |  0.1634 |                    1289 |
| + item count (numeric)              |          0.738 |            0.697 |  0.1643 |                    1524 |

Bootstrap 95% CI of the AUC change vs production: no customer history: -0.084 to -0.016; + 8 product flags: -0.005 to +0.021.

Decision: keep the reported history (available at order time, worth ~0.05 AUC, leakage not shown) but treat 'no history' as the robustness floor: it still nets positive while the ops rule loses heavily. Products: CI crosses zero and ₹ falls, so not added. Item count as a number: no gain over `single_item`. Before go-live, check the fields against OYTRA's own Shopify customer records.


## 10. Root cause of the history inconsistency (`python -m oytra.history_rootcause`)
- **Our parse/sort?** No. 2018/2018 timestamps share one format, 0 parse failures; we sort by parsed time with order_id as a stable tie-break. Prior-RTO decreases on 75 phones (the earlier figure of 74 is reproduced exactly when grouping by the raw phone string: 74; normalising '+91'/'0' prefixes joins one more customer. Same-minute ties don't change it: 75), prior-orders on 204.
- **One phone, different people?** No. Of 364 repeat phones only 6 carry more than one name and 5 more than one city (349 have different pincodes: same person, varying address). 122 name+city pairs appear on several phones, mostly common names, so name is not a key.
- **Counter reset?** Not cleanly: 215 drops, 182 to 0 (0 is 75% of all values anyway) and 33 to another non-zero value.
- **Source data: yes.** Sorted by timestamp, 204 phones have a falling count, about what random shuffling gives (173.4); prior RTO 75 vs 70.4. Sorted by **order_id**, only 61 of 507 steps go down (vs 215 by time) and the count is ≥ the order's position 93% of the time (vs 73%). Within a phone, a later timestamp has a higher order_id only 54% of the time. Single-order phones report 'first-time' 99.6% of the time.

**Verdict:** Source-data issue. Not our parsing or sorting (one timestamp format, 0 parse failures, stable time sort), not one phone shared by different people (same name/city on almost every repeat phone), and not a counter reset. The counts were accumulated in order_id order, but order_id and order_datetime disagree, so in time order they look scrambled. We keep time order (the backtest must be time-based) and treat the fields as reported signals, not exact counts. Because the order_id sequence may include orders dated later, the no-history model stays the worst case. Exposure: 7 of 329 September orders have a same-phone order with a lower ID but a later timestamp, so the possible look-ahead is small; the no-history model (section 9) stays the worst case.

**Identifying first-time customers reliably:** (1) At order time, look up the Shopify customer ID (customer.id / orders_count) from the order webhook; it is maintained by Shopify, not re-typed. (2) Fallback key: normalised phone (last 10 digits) + email, matched against OYTRA's own order table including orders still in transit. (3) Count prior RTOs from courier final statuses already received, never from the order payload. (4) Log the key used and the counts with each decision so they can be audited later.


## 11. Temporal leakage audit of the pincode/state encoding (`python -m oytra.leakage_audit`)
- Encoders used to score September are fit on Apr–Aug only (latest training date 2026-08-31 20:50:00). Flipping every September label leaves September scores unchanged: True.
- Training rows get a chronological (earlier-orders-only, weekly expanding) pin feature: 0 of 20 sampled rows move when their own label is flipped, and 0 earlier rows move when a later label is flipped. (without out-of-time encoding, training rows would see their own label: in-sample vs chronological pin feature correlation with RTO 0.576 vs 0.159.)
- CV for threshold choice re-fits encoders inside each fold: fold-0 predictions unchanged when fold-0 labels are flipped: True. Folds are random within Apr–Aug (random 5-fold inside Apr-Aug (not time-ordered); used only to choose thresholds).
- Label lag (production realism): only 1,491 of 1,658 training outcomes would be known 14 days before 1 Sep. Training on those only: September AUC 0.738 vs 0.738, net ₹1,522 vs ₹1,387.

**Verdict:** No September outcome reaches September scores; training rows use a chronological (earlier-orders-only) pincode encoding. No headline number changes. In production, retrain only on matured outcomes.


## 12. Evaluation metrics, September (329 orders, 86 RTO)
- ROC-AUC 0.738. **PR-AUC (average precision) 0.534** vs a base rate of 0.261 (what a random ranking would score).
- **Brier 0.1643** vs 0.1931 for always predicting the base rate.
- Majority-class accuracy 73.86%: context only. Saying 'delivered' to everyone is this accurate and saves ₹0, which is why we judge in ₹.

| Risk bucket | Orders | RTO | Mean predicted | Actual RTO rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0%–20% | 138 | 17 | 13.5% | 12.3% |
| 20%–40% | 139 | 41 | 28.6% | 29.5% |
| 40%–60% | 37 | 16 | 48.7% | 43.2% |
| 60%–87.5% | 14 | 11 | 69.7% | 78.6% |
| 87.5%+ | 1 | 1 | 93.0% | 100.0% |

Calibration chart: `reports/calibration.png` (SVG source `reports/calibration.svg`). The model is well calibrated in the buckets with enough orders; the top two buckets are small (16 and 2 orders).


## 13. Feature ablation (`python -m oytra.ablation`, full table in `reports/ablation.md`)
Same Apr–Aug → Sep split, same thresholds; one feature or group removed at a time.

| Variant | AUC | ΔAUC | PR-AUC | Brier | Sep net ₹ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| full model (production) | 0.738 | +0.000 | 0.534 | 0.1643 | 1,387 |
| group: customer history (reported) | 0.689 | -0.049 | 0.500 | 0.1716 | 1,452 |
| group: area (pincode/state RTO rate) | 0.693 | -0.045 | 0.512 | 0.1698 | 1,425 |
| group: address / name / phone quality | 0.683 | -0.055 | 0.451 | 0.1761 | 2,073 |
| group: order value + night-time | 0.727 | -0.011 | 0.525 | 0.1665 | 1,866 |
| group: basket (single item) | 0.733 | -0.005 | 0.524 | 0.1664 | 1,522 |

Reading: address/name/phone quality, area (pincode/state) and reported customer history each carry ~0.04–0.06 AUC; value+night ~0.01; single features like `night`, `name_fake` (also a hard rule) and `phone_invalid` add ~nothing to AUC. ₹ moves by a few hundred either way, within one month's noise, and sometimes rises when AUC falls (the hard address/name rules still act on those orders). No feature is removed on one month's evidence; `phone_invalid` is the first candidate to drop if the next month agrees.
